full_judgment:
Ahsanuddin Chowdhury, J— This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the order dated 13.1.73 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dacca in T. S. No. 288 of 1967 rejecting the prayer for certain amendment in paragraph 10 of the Addle Written Statement filed in that suit by the petitioner should not be set aside. 

 2. The rule arises in the following circumstances:—The opposite parties as plaintiffs have instituted a Suit being Title Suit No 288 of 1967 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca for a declaration of their raiyati right in respect of 16 annas share in the suit property and also for a declaration that the notice No. 536 (18) V-2/67 dated 15-6-67 issued by the Member, Board of Revenue and all subsequent actions taken by him are illegal, void and without jurisdiction. The plaint case is that the suit land was the Khas land of the Bhowal Estate and on the prayer of one Torah Ali and 16 others the Khas land was settled with them by the Bhowal Estate at annual dental of Taka 1500 in the year 1344 B.S. and since their settlement they were in possession demarcating the boundaries. Some of the plaintiffs are transferors from the Original settlement holders. During the State Acquisition Settlement Operation the suit land was illegally recorded in the name of the defendant petitioner. Whereupon the plaintiff-opposite parties filed a petition under section 143 of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act for correction of the record and thereafter the Sub divisional Manager, Sadar South, on the recommendation of the Circle Inspector and Tahsilder submitted a proposal to the A.D C. (Revenue, for recognition of the tenancy-right of the puff opposite parties and the A. D.C. (Rev.) recognized their said right and realised rent from them. Thereafter the Board of Revenue passed an order cancelling the recognition of the tenancy right of the plffs. and declaring that the aid land was the Khas land of the Bhowal Estate and after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it became the Khas land of the Government In the meantime the entire land was acquired under the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 by the Govt. and compensation was paid to some of the plaintiff ; But the order of the Board of Revenue having cast some cloud on their title, they have instituted the above mentioned suit. Thereafter, at a certain stage of the suit the plaint was amended. After the amendment of the plaint the defendant-petitioner filed an additional written statement; subsequently defendant petitioner wanted to make some amendments in paragraph 10 of the additional written statement. Accordingly prayer was made on a verified petition for amendments to be made in paragraph 10 of the additional written statement. But the learned Subordinate Judge rejected the prayer for amendment on the ground that the amendment, if allowed, would prejudice the plaintiff-opposite parties. Thereafter the present rule was obtained by the defdt.- petitioner. 

 3. In order to have a clear view of the amendment sought to be made, paragraph 10 of the additional written statement is produced below:- 

 "That the allegations made in paragraphs 10-12 of the petition are not at all true or correct. With the requisition and acquisition the property vested in the Govt and the Govt is entitled to take possession the same in payment of provisional compensation to the owners and the real owners have already been paid compensation. The plffs. are nothing but illegal occupants and trespassers after the Requisition and acquisition of the land. The Government can evict the trespassers by the help of Act X of 1953 or by section 12 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act and the plaintiffs cannot resist the Government under the law." 

 4. By the proposed amendment in paragraph 10 of the additional written statement the words. “With the requisition and acquisition the property vested if the Government and the Govt. is entitled to take possession of the same on payment of provisional compensation to the owners and the real owners have already been paid compensation" occurring in the above quoted paragraph 10 are to be deleted and to be replaced by the words:- 

 "That the allegations made in paragraphs 10-12 of the petition are not at all true or correct. Some of the plaintiffs have been paid compensation as per provisional Award prepared by the L A. Collector before the receipt of the cancellation order of the Senior Member, Board of Revenue, cancelling the entry in C S Plot No. 401 in the Collector's Khatian in the record of right. The Plaintiffs are not entitled to take advantage of this wrong payment, as the plaintiffs have acquired no right, title or interest over the suit property nor their alleged vendors had any right, title or interest over the suit property. The plaintiffs are nothing but illegal occupants and trespassers after the requisition and acquisition of the kind, The Government can evict the trespassers by the help of Act X of 1953 or by section 12 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act and the plaintiffs cannot resist the Government under the Law." 

 5. Mr. Moinul Huq contends that the amendment asked for should not be allowed because the amendment if allowed will take away the admissions already made by the defendant petitioner in paragraph 10 of the additional written statement and that it is not correct to say that the proposed amendment merely seeks to cancel a statement made through inadvertence nor is it correct to say that the statements sought to be deleted are contrary to the Govt. record. 

 8. Mr. Ranadhir Sen has argued that by the amendment, if allowed, no prejudice will be caused to the plaintiff-opposite parties. Rather the amendment will help determination of the real question in controversy between the parties. The plaintiff opposite parties claim their tenancy right in the suit land on the basis of settlement of their vendors from the Bhowal Estate while the case of the defendant-petitioner is that the land was Khas land of the Bhowal Estate and after the acquisition under the Acquisition and deviancy Act the suit land became the Khas land of the Government as it was not found retainable by the ex-landlord. Mr. Sen further states that at certain stage the land was acquired under the Emergency Requisition Act and some of the plaintiffs got compensation but from this payment of compensation it cannot be said that their ownership was admitted in the land. The compensation might have been paid on the basis of possession. But inadvertently it was stated in para 10 of written statement that provisional compensation was paid to the owners of the land. It seems Mr. Ranadhir Sen has argued rightly that the statement that provisional compensation was paid to the owners of the land was made through inadvertence and that it was nothing but a bonfire mistake which is now sought to be deleted by the proposed amendment. In the khatian also the possession of some of the plaintiffs appears to have been recorded with the remark ‘No title to the land’. In this view of the matter Mr. Ranadhir Sen, we think, has rightly argued that the amendment, if allowed, will not cause any prejudice to any claim of the plaintiff opposite parties. 

 9. Mr. Moinul Huq, on the other hand, contends that in paragraph 10 of the written statement the plaintiff opposite parties have been admitted to be the real owners of the land and this admission has been affirmed by the final award made by the Collector under the Land Acquisition Act. But by the proposed amendment the defendant petitioner wants to recile from their admission. As such the amendment should not be allowed we find no force in this argument and this will be borne out if the whole of the paragraph 10 of the additional written statement is taken into consideration. The plffs. were not stated in the paragraph to be the owners. They have been described as illegal occupants and trespassers in the land. 

 12. Mr. Ranadhir Sen has referred us to some decisions in support of the rule for amendment sought to be made in paragraph 10 of the additional written statement. These cases are. AIR. 1922. (Cal.)-255, AIR. 1930 (Allahabad)-474, A.I.R. 1953 (Cal.)-15, A.I.R 1956 (Cal) 630 and 15 DLR (SC) 20. All these cases except the one reported in AIR 1953 (Cal.) 15, are in respect of amendment of plaint. In all these cases it has been held that under Order VI, rule 17 the Court has been given the discretion to allow either party at any stage of the proceedings to alter or amend his pleading in such a manner and on such terms as they be just and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties. It is apparent that no particular principle except what has been provided under Order VI rule 17 C P.C. has been laid down in these cases. These cases have, therefore, no special significance to the petitioner's prayer for amendment of the written statement. A.I R. 1953 (Cal.)-15, however, relates to amendments of written statement. It is to be noted that amendment of a plaint and amendment of a written statement are not necessarily governed by exactly the same principles. Some important general principles are no doubt common to both, such as the application for amendment whether of a plaint or a written statement must be bonafide and must also be for the purpose of determining the real controversy between the parties and where it is just. But the rule that the plff. cannot be allowed to amend his plaint so as to alter materially or substitute his cause of action or the nature of his claim has necessarily no counterpart in the law relating to amendment of the defence or the written statement. The governing consideration in an application to amend the written statement should be how far, if at all, the proposed amendment of the defence is necessary to determine the real controversy between the parties. It is thus evident that the Court has the positive duty to decide whether the proposed amendment is necessary to determine the real controversy between the parties. If that test is satisfied the amendment shall be allowed, otherwise not. This view has been expressed in A I.R. 1953 (Cal)15. 

 13. On the other hand, Mr Moinul Huq opposing the proposed amendment has relied upon some decisions namely. Indian Cases-267 XXIX in Indian Cases-355, 80 Indian Cases-355 and XLVIII ILR (Cal) 832. In IX I.C. it has been held that the exercise of the power of a court to allow pleadings and issues to be amended under Order VI. Rule 17 C.P.C. is discretionary and in the discretion cannot he interfered with under section 70 (1) (a) of the Punjab Courts Act until it is shown to have blend exercised. It appears that wan the particular enactment, namely Punjab Courts Act; the above observation was made in the ease by the learned Judge. In XXIX Indian Cases it has been observed that the High Court ought not to interfere with the discretion deliberately exercised by a lower court in refusing to allow a plaintiff to amend his plaint during the progress of the suit, unless it is satisfied that the lower court came to a wrong conclusion. In 80 I.C. the plaintiff sued to reactive possession of a holding alleging that he was an occupancy tenant of the holding and was disposed by the defendant in July, 1920. The defendant contended that the plff. had been out of possession since 1918 and had surrendered his tenancy and that the defdt had been placed in possession by the Malaguzer. In the course of the pleading the plff. stated through his pleader that he had been out of possession since the end of 1918. In reply it was pleaded that the plff not having been in possession of the land within 2 years from the date of the suit, his claim was barred by limitation under Article 1 of Schedule 11 to the C.P. tenancy Act of 1920. On the fixed for hearing arguments on the point of limitation the plff applied to amend his pleadings on the ground that he inadvertently stated that he was dispossessed in 1918. His prayer for amendment in respect of the date of dispossession was net allowed in order to get out of the effect of his own admission which was very relevant on the point of limitation. Mr. Moinul Huq has very much relied on this decision in opposing the amendment sought for in the instant case. But the facts of the case under reference and those of the instant case are different. Furthermore in this case under reference the question of special limitation was involved. In I.L.R. XLVIII (Cal)-832 (Privy Council), the appellant contracted in 1903 to sell to the respondent three out of twelve sites for oil wells which she expected to be allowed to her by Govt. for that year. In 1904, four sites were allotted under the contract of 1903, but the appellant did not obtain the whole twelve till 1912. The respondent in 1904 or 1905 after the four sites were allotted asked the appellant to transfer these to him but she refused; no sites were transferred to him. In 1913 the appellant sued the respondent for specific performance of a verbal agreement which he alleged that the appellant had made in 1912 in reference to the 1903 contract to transfer to him three sites allotted in 1912, but not being among those allotted in 1903. Both courts found against the alleged verbal agreement, but the appellate court allowed the respondent to amend his plaint by claiming damages for the failure to deliver sites under the agreement of 1903. It was held, that it was not open to the court under section 153 and Order VI, rule 17 to allow the amendment, as it altered the real matter in controversy between the parties and also on the ground that the claim as amended was barred by limitation. 

 14. There is no dispute with regard to the principles laid down in the above mentioned cases. In the instant case proposed amendment if made, will not change the nature of the suit, rather it will help the determination of the real question in controversy between the parties. It may also be noted in this connection that the plff opp. parties have instituted the suit merely for a declaration that they have tenancy right in the suit land. Thereafter they got the plaint amended and the amendment consists of 18 paragraphs. The amendment of the plaint in such as extensive manner made it necessary for the defendant petitioner to file additional written statement. In paragraph 10 of the additional written statement some persons who were paid some compensation for the acquisition of some land of the plaint schedule were described as the owners of the land. This statement it is said, was an inadvertent one and as such has been sought to be deleted by way of amendment. It is to be decided whether by mere payment of compensation to some persons found in possession, they necessarily become the owner thereof the title and for the matter of that, the ownership is to be established on legal evidence. The parties are already in litigation over the title of the land and the said dispute will be decided by the court legal and proper evidence. The plffs. Opposite parties can have no reason for being prejudiced inasmuch as they are not debarred, in view of the proposed amendment from giving evidence in the suit before the court to prove their title to the land? 

 In view of the facts and circumstances giving rise to this litigation we are of the view that for the purpose of determining the real question in controversy between the parties the proposed amendment should be allowed in the result the rule is made absolute. It is directed that the amendment sought for be made in paragraph 10 of the additional written statement in the manner indicated in the amendment application before this Court we do not however make any order as to costs.
